title: Written in Stone
description: Read the clues in crystals, textures, and the conditions that turn one rock into another.

questions.prompt: Sandstone is made mainly from grains of what material?
questions.hint: Its name records the size of the particles that became rock.
questions.explanation: Sandstone forms when sand grains are compacted and cemented together.

questions.prompt: What must happen to molten material for an igneous rock to form?

questions.hint: The key change is between physical states.
questions.explanation: Igneous rocks form when molten rock cools and becomes solid, either underground or at the surface.

questions.prompt: Why can a fresh piece of pumice sometimes float on water?

choices.text: Its crystals are made of frozen gas
Its many gas cavities lower its bulk density

questions.hint: Consider the volume occupied by the solid material and the holes together.
questions.explanation: Pumice contains many vesicles left by gas. These can make its overall density lower than water's.

questions.prompt: In Bowen's discontinuous reaction series, which mineral normally crystallizes at the highest temperature?
questions.hint: The early mineral is common in magnesium- and iron-rich mantle rocks.
questions.explanation: Olivine lies at the high-temperature end of the discontinuous series, followed on cooling by pyroxene, amphibole, and biotite.

questions.prompt: An undisturbed uranium-lead date from a zircon that grew in cooling magma primarily dates which event?

choices.text: The creation of uranium in the Solar System
The deposition of any sediment later covering it
The first exposure of the rock at the surface

questions.hint: The clock belongs to the mineral, not automatically to every later event affecting the landscape.
questions.explanation: A magmatic zircon records its crystallization age if its isotopic system remains undisturbed. That can date formation of the igneous body.

questions.prompt: Basalt and gabbro can have similar mineral composition but different crystal sizes. Which contrast best explains this?

choices.text: Basalt cools rapidly; gabbro cools slowly
Basalt cools slowly; gabbro cools rapidly
Basalt is recrystallized gabbro formed without melting
Gabbro is compacted basaltic sediment formed without melting

questions.hint: Composition and cooling history describe different properties of a rock.
questions.explanation: Basalt is the fine-grained volcanic counterpart of coarse-grained intrusive gabbro. Their contrasting cooling rates explain the textures.

questions.prompt: At a given pressure, adding water to hot mantle rock generally has which effect?

choices.text: It prevents partial melting while allowing total melting
It lowers the temperature at which melting begins
It raises the temperature at which melting begins
It leaves the onset unchanged but stops crystallization

questions.hint: Subducting material carries an ingredient that changes the melting threshold.
questions.explanation: Water lowers the solidus of mantle rock, helping generate magma above subduction zones.

questions.prompt: Graphite is thermodynamically favored over diamond at ordinary surface conditions. Why can a diamond nevertheless persist?

choices.text: Conversion can occur only after all carbon melts
The pressure of formation remains trapped in every bond
Conversion requires overcoming a large kinetic barrier
Cooling removes the thermodynamic preference for graphite

questions.hint: A favorable final state does not tell you how quickly a material can reach it.
questions.explanation: Diamond is metastable at ordinary conditions. Rearranging its strongly bonded structure into graphite is so slow that the diamond persists.

metadata.author: OpenAI
metadata.verificationNotes: Reviewed distinction between thermodynamic preference and reaction kinetics; no claim that diamond is the equilibrium carbon phase at room conditions.
